prompt: `files.py` printed `1536.0 per vector` for both `v384.npy` and `flat384.faiss`. What does that tell you about a flat file?
hint: Compare it with the bytes in memory on the line above.

choices.text: It holds the numbers and almost nothing else besides a short header
choices.why: Right. 4 × 384 is 1,536, and the few bytes of header each format adds disappear when spread over 20,000 vectors.

choices.text: FAISS and NumPy compress the vectors to the same size while writing them
choices.why: Neither compresses anything here: both files equal the in-memory size, 30,720,000 bytes, plus a small header.

choices.text: The size depends on the random values synth.py happened to draw
choices.why: A float32 takes four bytes whatever it holds, which is why the lesson could measure sizes on random vectors at all.

choices.text: A flat FAISS index stores each vector together with its neighbours
choices.why: That is a graph index. A flat index is a plain list of vectors, compared one by one at search time.

prompt: For the 1536-dimension table, `sizes.sql` showed `heap` 1,212,416 bytes and `toast` 163,840,000. Why is the heap so small?
hint: How big is one vector of 1536 float32 numbers, and how big is a page?

choices.text: pgvector compressed the vectors inside the heap
choices.why: pgvector 0.6.0 declares its type STORAGE external: moved out of the row and never compressed. The bytes are in toast, not shrunk.

choices.text: The vectors had not been loaded yet when sizes.sql ran
choices.why: load.py had already printed 20000 rows for v1536, and sizes.sql counted 20000 too.

choices.text: Each vector is too large for the row, so it lives out of line
choices.why: Right. Over 6 KB of numbers cannot share an 8 KB page, so PostgreSQL moves it to TOAST storage and keeps a pointer in the row.

choices.text: VACUUM ANALYZE moved the vectors into the primary key index
choices.why: An index on id holds ids. The indexes column was 466,944 bytes for both tables, far too small to hold the vectors.

prompt: A model returns 1024 numbers per text as float32. How many bytes does one vector take in a flat file, leaving out the file's header?
hint: A float32 is four bytes, and a flat file adds nothing per vector.

prompt: When a pgvector value is too big to stay in its row, PostgreSQL moves it out of line into the table's ___ storage and leaves a pointer behind.
hint: It is the column that held 163,840,000 bytes for the 1536-dimension table.

prompt: The HNSW index on `v384` came to 2,048 bytes a row, more than the table's 1,676. What is in it?
hint: To compare a query with a vector, the index needs something.

choices.text: A copy of each vector and the links to its neighbours
choices.why: Right. pgvector keeps the vector inside the index next to its graph links, so the index is another copy plus the links.

choices.text: The text of each row, so that results can be shown without the table
choices.why: The table has no text column at all, only id and embedding, and the index still outweighs it.

choices.text: Every vector stored as float64, which doubles its size
choices.why: Doubling 1,536 would give over 3,000 bytes a row. The index keeps the same four-byte numbers.

choices.text: One small entry per dimension, 384 of them per row
choices.why: An HNSW index has one element per vector, not per coordinate; the size comes from the vector and its links.

prompt: hnswlib's file was 1.10 times the flat file at 384 dimensions and 1.02 times at 1536, with the same `M`. Why does the ratio fall?
hint: What does M decide, and does it depend on the dimension?

choices.text: hnswlib keeps fewer links for longer vectors
choices.why: The number of links is set by M, which was 16 in both runs; the dimension does not change it.

choices.text: The links take about the same bytes per vector at any size
choices.why: Right. A fixed cost per vector weighs a tenth against 1,536 bytes and much less against 6,144.

choices.text: Longer vectors compress better when hnswlib saves them
choices.why: Nothing is compressed: the 1536 file is 6,292.6 bytes a vector, more than its 6,144 bytes of numbers.

choices.text: The 1536-dimension index was built with a smaller ef_construction
choices.why: graphs.py uses ef_construction=64 for both, and that parameter affects build quality and time, not the stored size.

prompt: A team wants an HNSW index on text-embedding-3-large's 3072-number vectors in the lab's pgvector 0.6.0, without upgrading. What gets them an index?
hint: The error named a limit. Which of these changes the thing it limits?

choices.text: Raise maintenance_work_mem until the build has room
choices.why: Memory changes how fast a build runs. The refusal was about the column: more than 2000 dimensions for hnsw.

choices.text: Store the column as halfvec to halve its size
choices.why: halfvec arrived in pgvector 0.7.0. The lab's 0.6.0 has only vector, stored as float32.

choices.text: Shorten the vectors to 2,000 numbers or fewer
choices.why: Right. With the dimensions parameter or by truncating and renormalising, the column fits the limit; lesson 7 and section 04 measured what shortening costs.

choices.text: Use vector_l2_ops instead of vector_cosine_ops
choices.why: The operator class picks the distance. The dimension limit applies to the index whatever distance it uses.

prompt: Match each way of keeping the 20,000 vectors of 384 dimensions to the bytes per vector this lesson measured for it.
hint: The flat file is the floor; pgvector's index holds the vector plus links.

prompt: Storing the vectors as float16 halved their bytes. How much of the full-size neighbourhood did that keep?
hint: Read the top-10 kept column on the float16 rows.

choices.text: About half, in step with the bytes
choices.why: That is the proportional picture the section set out to test. Halving the bytes this way moved almost nothing.

choices.text: All of it for MiniLM, 0.999 for WordLlama
choices.why: Right. float16 keeps enough precision that each text's ten nearest neighbours stay put.

choices.text: None of the 24 questions could be answered any more
choices.why: Both models answered the 24 questions exactly as with float32: 19 and 22 for MiniLM, 20 and 24 for WordLlama.

choices.text: 0.705 for MiniLM and 0.600 for WordLlama
choices.why: Those are the binary rows, one bit per number, not the float16 ones.

prompt: As binary, MiniLM's `r@3` went from 22/24 to 23/24, while it kept only 0.705 of its top-10 neighbours. What should you conclude?
hint: How many questions does r@3 count, and how many texts does the other column cover?

choices.text: Binary vectors search better than float32 for this model
choices.why: Nearly a third of each text's neighbours changed. One extra question in 24 is within what chance moves.

choices.text: The 24 questions are too few to see the change
choices.why: Right. The neighbour measure, over every text in the set, saw it clearly; a small judged set could not.

choices.text: The float32 measurement had a bug that binary fixed
choices.why: float32 is the reference both columns are built from, and it reproduced lesson 3's 19 and 22.

choices.text: Binary keeps the same neighbours, so recall can only stay or rise
choices.why: It kept 0.705 of them, so about three in ten neighbours were different.

prompt: You can spend about 256 bytes per vector on WordLlama. Going by `shrink.py`, which choice keeps the most of the full-size neighbourhood?
hint: Several rows cost about 256 bytes. Compare their last column.

choices.text: The first 64 dimensions, kept as float32
choices.why: 256 bytes and 0.642 kept: cutting numbers cost far more than cutting bits did.

choices.text: Any of them, since equal bytes carry equal information
choices.why: The rows near 256 bytes kept between 0.642 and 0.995, so equal bytes are not equal neighbourhoods.

choices.text: The first 128 dimensions, kept as float16
choices.why: 256 bytes and 0.772 kept: better than 64 dimensions, still well short of the full 256 dimensions in int8.

choices.text: All 256 dimensions as int8
choices.why: Right. 260 bytes and 0.995 kept. At the same size, fewer bits per number beat fewer numbers on this model.

prompt: MiniLM's 384 numbers are stored as int8, one byte each, plus one float32 scale per vector, as `shrink.py` does. How many bytes per vector is that?
hint: Count the scale too: a float32 is four bytes.

prompt: Order these forms of WordLlama's vectors by how much of the full 256-dimension neighbourhood they kept, from most to least.
hint: Bits per number cost little until binary; dimensions cost at every step.
trap: 256 dimensions as binary is not above 64 as float32: 0.600 against 0.642, even though binary keeps every dimension.

prompt: `reembed.py` priced a million texts like the lab's at $0.45 on text-embedding-3-small. What does that say about moving a corpus to a new model?
hint: Compare that figure with the other two bills the section names.

choices.text: The token bill is rarely the part that makes a migration expensive
choices.why: Right. Re-embedding is dollars per million short texts; the new index and the double storage are the larger costs.

choices.text: Migrations are cheap overall, since tokens are the whole cost
choices.why: Tokens are one of three bills. The index has to be built again and both sets of vectors are stored for a while.

choices.text: Hosted models are always cheaper than running one locally
choices.why: The local model has no bill at all, only time: 2.8 hours on one core for the same million.

choices.text: Longer chunks would cost the same, since the price is per text
choices.why: The price is per token, so chunks ten times longer cost ten times as much.

prompt: In `rebuild.py`, eight times the vectors took 4.76 s against 0.54 s. Why does an HNSW build not get cheaper per vector as it grows?
hint: What does adding one vector to the graph involve?

choices.text: hnswlib uses fewer threads for bigger indexes
choices.why: Nothing in rebuild.py sets the threads, and the machine had the same 4 cores for every size.

choices.text: Each insertion is a search in a graph that keeps growing
choices.why: Right. Every vector added has to find its neighbours among all those already inserted, so later ones cost more.

choices.text: Random vectors are harder to place than real embeddings
choices.why: All four sizes use the same kind of vectors, so that would not change the cost per vector between them.

choices.text: The file has to be written again after every insertion
choices.why: rebuild.py never saves the index; the time is the build alone.

prompt: A search moves from MiniLM (384 dimensions) to a 1536-dimension model in pgvector with HNSW, without going offline. What do you have to store while it moves?
hint: The reads move only once the new index is ready.

choices.text: Only the new rows; the old ones can be dropped as soon as the backfill starts
choices.why: The old rows and index are what is serving searches until the new index is built and the reads switch.

choices.text: Only the old rows, until a single moment when every vector is converted to 1536 dimensions
choices.why: A 384-number vector cannot be converted into a 1536-number one; every text has to be embedded again by the new model.

choices.text: Both models' rows and indexes
choices.why: Right. From 1,676 + 2,048 bytes a row to 8,371 + 8,192, and during the move you hold the sum.

choices.text: The new rows, with the old index kept to answer queries
choices.why: An index built on 384-dimension vectors cannot search 1536-dimension ones, and it holds its own copy of the old vectors anyway.

prompt: `tombstones.py` deleted every other vector from the hnswlib index and saved it again. What happened to the file?
hint: Compare the built and deleted lines.

choices.text: It halved, since half the vectors were gone
choices.why: The file stayed at 33,691,896 bytes. hnswlib does not take a deleted vector out of the graph.

choices.text: It grew, because each deletion is logged
choices.why: The size was exactly the same before and after. Nothing is added for a deletion beyond a mark.

choices.text: It stayed the same size
choices.why: Right. The deleted vectors are only marked; searches skip them, but they keep their slots and their bytes.

choices.text: It was rewritten without the deleted ids and then padded back to size
choices.why: There is no rewrite. The count stayed at 20000 elements because the marked ones are still in the index.

prompt: In `vacuum.sql`, VACUUM took `128811.541 ms` and every size stayed the same. What did that time buy?
hint: What does VACUUM have to do inside an HNSW index for each dead row?

choices.text: Nothing yet: VACUUM only schedules the cleanup for later
choices.why: VACUUM does the work when it runs. What it does not do is give the freed space back.

choices.text: It removed the dead entries and repaired the links that pointed at them
choices.why: Right. The freed space stays inside the files for new rows, so the sizes do not change; a REINDEX is what shrank them.

choices.text: It rebuilt both indexes from the 10,000 remaining rows
choices.why: That is what REINDEX did, in 6291.040 ms, and it halved the indexes.

choices.text: It returned the freed pages to the operating system
choices.why: Plain VACUUM keeps the space for reuse inside the table and indexes; the heap stayed at 32,768,000 bytes.

prompt: Two models both return 768 numbers. The alias is switched to the new model's collection, but the code still embeds questions with the old model. What happens?
hint: In `alias.py` the mismatch failed because 384 is not 256.

choices.text: Qdrant refuses the query with a shape error
choices.why: That happened in alias.py only because the dimensions differed. At 768 against 768 the arithmetic works.

choices.text: The alias rejects queries from a different model
choices.why: An alias is a name for a collection. It knows nothing about which model produced a query vector.

choices.text: Results come back with no error, and they are wrong
choices.why: Right. The vectors of two models are not comparable, so the scores measure nothing while looking normal. That is why the model's name travels with the version.

choices.text: The scores are a little lower, but the order is the same
choices.why: Coordinates of two models have nothing to do with each other, so there is no reason the order would survive.

prompt: hnswlib does not take a deleted vector out of its graph; it only marks it, which leaves what is called a ___.
hint: A marker over something that is gone.

prompt: Put in order the steps of moving a search to a new model without taking it offline.
hint: The alias moves only when the new collection can answer.
items: Create a new versioned collection for the new model
Embed every document with the new model into it
Point the alias and the query embedding at the new version
trap: Pointing the alias before the index is built sends searches to a collection that cannot answer yet; deleting the old one before the switch leaves nothing serving.

prompt: In the budget for two million chunks, which part has to fit in memory for searches to stay fast?
hint: A search hops through one structure page by page.

choices.text: The HNSW index, 16.38 GB
choices.why: Right. A search walks the graph from page to page, and every page not in memory is a read from disk.

choices.text: The token bill, $12.00
choices.why: That is money paid once to the provider, not something held in memory.

choices.text: The text of the chunks
choices.why: The text is fetched only for the few results returned; the search itself walks the index.

choices.text: The raw float32 vectors, 12.29 GB, kept as a separate file
choices.why: In this budget the vectors live in Postgres; the raw figure is what the numbers alone would take, not a separate copy to load.

prompt: The sheet's batch price for text-embedding-3-large is $0.065 per million tokens. What would embedding the two million chunks of 300 tokens cost at that price, in dollars?
hint: budget.py counted the tokens: 600,000,000.

prompt: A stable name that the application searches, pointed at whichever versioned collection is live, is what Qdrant calls an ___.
hint: alias.py switches one from help_v1 to help_v2.

prompt: Match each way of shrinking WordLlama's 256 float32 numbers to what `shrink.py` measured for it.
hint: Two of them cost the same bytes and keep very different neighbourhoods.

pairs.right: About a quarter of the bytes, 0.995 kept
A thirty-second of the bytes, 0.600 kept
A quarter of the bytes, 0.642 kept

prompt: Which of these make the monthly storage of a vector store in pgvector smaller? Choose all that apply.
hint: Monthly storage is rows times bytes per row, for every copy kept.

choices.text: A model, or a setting, with fewer dimensions
choices.why: Yes. Every byte line scales with the dimension, in the table and in the index.

choices.text: REINDEX after a large share of rows has been deleted
choices.why: Yes. In vacuum.sql it halved both indexes, where VACUUM alone changed no size.

choices.text: Paying the batch price for the first embedding
choices.why: That halves a one-off token bill. It stores nothing less.

choices.text: Running VACUUM after every delete
choices.why: VACUUM keeps the freed space inside the files for reuse; every size stayed the same after it.
